description: Short, continuously updated plain-language overview of where ME/CFS research stands, shown on the dashboard's Overview tab and rendered to STATE-OF-THE-ART.md. It is a synthesis of the confirmed entries in data/papers.json and data/trials.json — every point cites their ids in `refs`, and nothing may be claimed that those entries do not support. STYLE: layperson language as in papers.json; one-sentence `takeaway` per section; 2–6 `points` per section, each ≤ ~45 words; replace outdated points rather than appending. `confidence` is one of: established, strong, emerging, contested, early. Bump a section's `updated` (and top-level `updated`) only when its content changes; set top-level `reviewed` every run. Optional `keywords` (lower-case substrings matched against paper titles + summaries) assign papers to a section's topic for the Papers-tab topic filter; cited `refs` are always included. See ROUTINE.md → 'State of the art'. Also holds `model` (the 'how it may fit together' diagram: rows of nodes, each linked to a section) and `treatments` (the treatment board: result = promising | negative | testing, a short `note`, cited `refs`); keep both in sync with the sections. Each section has a `short_title` for its tile.
intro: A short, plain-language summary of what research currently shows about ME/CFS, built only from the papers and trials tracked on this page and revised as new results come in.

model.title: How the pieces may fit together
model.caption: One leading model, from Wirth and Scheibenbogen, of how the findings may connect. Parts are well supported, others are still being tested — and not every patient may fit it.

sections.title: What ME/CFS is
sections.takeaway: A serious, long-lasting physical illness whose defining feature is a crash after even small amounts of activity.

points.text: The hallmark is post-exertional malaise (PEM): symptoms get markedly worse after physical or mental effort, often with a delay. Modern diagnostic criteria put PEM at the centre.
PEM can be measured objectively: on two exercise tests 24 hours apart, patients cannot repeat their first-day performance.
Roughly 0.5–1% of people are affected worldwide, depending on the definition used.
Many cases start after an infection. After COVID-19, about one in five people in a large New York survey reported PEM, and post-COVID patients increasingly resemble established ME/CFS over time.
International experts have now agreed on a common way to measure the core symptoms, which should make studies easier to compare.

sections.title: Genes: a real biological basis
sections.takeaway: Large genetic studies show ME/CFS has a real, inherited component that points mainly to the nervous and immune systems.

points.text: DecodeME, the largest genetic study so far (over 15,000 patients), found eight DNA regions linked to ME/CFS, several involved in fighting infection.
Independent groups have since replicated gene hits in other datasets, with the strongest signals in brain and nerve-signalling genes rather than blood.

Genetic analyses suggest ME/CFS has its own roots in nerve cells and is not simply a form of depression, even though symptoms can overlap; in a cohort followed after infection, inherited depression risk did not predict who developed a CFS-like post-infective illness.
Genetic ‘cause-and-effect’ methods point to cellular energy production and low-grade inflammation and clotting as likely causes, not just consequences, of the illness.

sections.title: Immune system & autoantibodies
sections.takeaway: The immune system is clearly involved, and ‘self-attacking’ antibodies are a leading theory — but removing them has so far given mixed results.

points.text: Many patients carry autoantibodies (antibodies that mistakenly target the body’s own receptors) against receptors that control blood vessels and nerves. This is the basis of the Scheibenbogen group’s autoimmune model.
Lab evidence that such antibodies can do harm: patients’ antibodies damaged cells’ energy machinery, and long-COVID antibodies caused symptoms when transferred into mice.
The ‘first-response’ (innate) immune system tends to overreact, and a calcium channel in immune cells (TRPM3) is faulty — a finding confirmed across several labs.

Filtering antibodies out of the blood (immunoadsorption) lowered antibody levels but did not beat a sham treatment in a German post-COVID trial; another small study was also negative. Two Berlin studies are still following it in antibody-positive patients.

Wiping out B cells with rituximab failed in a large trial, but targeting the antibody-making plasma cells (daratumumab) helped 6 of 10 patients in a small pilot. Charité plans a placebo-controlled B-cell trial (inebilizumab).

sections.title: Blood vessels & circulation
sections.takeaway: Poorly working small blood vessels and disturbed blood flow are among the most consistent findings.

points.text: The inner lining of blood vessels (endothelium) works poorly in many patients; a simple eye scan showed this was worst in the ME/CFS group of post-COVID patients.
During exercise, blood does not return to the heart properly (‘preload failure’), and muscles struggle to use the oxygen they receive.
Dizziness and a racing heart on standing (orthostatic intolerance, POTS) are common — over a third of teenagers with ME/CFS in one study had POTS.
Whether low blood volume drives this is debated: Wirth proposes it does, while a new measurement study found blood volume made no difference to who was affected.

‘Microclots’ (tiny, hard-to-dissolve clots) that may clog small vessels are reported in long COVID and ME/CFS — a theory with growing lab evidence, but not yet tested as a treatment target in the trials tracked here.

sections.title: Muscles & energy production
sections.takeaway: Muscles and cells’ energy supply are genuinely affected — this is where the Wirth/Scheibenbogen drug MDC002 aims.

points.text: Wirth and Scheibenbogen’s theory: too little blood flow lets sodium and then calcium build up in muscle cells, damaging their energy units (mitochondria) and causing the crash after activity.
Muscle biopsies differ from people after 60 days of bed rest — so the muscle changes are not just from being inactive.
Blood chemistry points to a ‘low-energy survival mode’ and a blocked step in turning food into energy; brain scans show extra lactate, a sign of energy made without enough oxygen.
Not everything holds up: a careful repeat of a well-known study found no ‘blood factor’ that disturbs healthy muscle cells.
MDC002 (Mitodicure, Klaus Wirth) is designed to break this calcium-overload cycle in muscle. A first trial in humans is planned but not yet registered.

sections.title: Brain & nervous system
sections.takeaway: Brain scans and spinal-fluid tests show measurable changes, but it is still unclear which of them drive the illness.

points.text: Fatigue appears to start partly in the brain: when muscles tire, the brain’s compensating signal barely increases in ME/CFS.
Brain chemistry is altered: spinal fluid shows too little activity of noradrenaline (an alertness messenger), and the stress hormone cortisol is consistently low.
The brain’s nightly ‘cleaning system’ seems weaker, which matches worse sleep and brain fog.
Brain inflammation is not settled: an early scan study found signs of it, while a recent post-COVID study found no immune attack inside the brain.

sections.title: Viruses & triggers
sections.takeaway: Infections, and dormant viruses ‘waking up’, are a likely trigger — but antiviral treatment has not helped so far.

points.text: Common dormant viruses (like Epstein-Barr virus and HHV-6) often reactivate during severe COVID-19, and this has been linked to later long COVID.
Leftover pieces of coronavirus have been found in gut tissue of long-COVID patients.
Yet the largest antiviral trial (Paxlovid) showed no benefit, and a drug against ‘fossil virus’ proteins in our DNA (temelimab) also failed.

sections.title: Gut
sections.takeaway: Gut problems are common and linked to overall severity; treating the gut is an early but plausible idea.

points.text: About one in three patients also has irritable bowel syndrome, and worse gut symptoms go along with worse ME/CFS symptoms and more inflammation.
Patients lack some ‘good’ bacteria, including ones that make a fuel for the gut lining.
A small placebo-controlled trial of a probiotic reduced fatigue in long COVID; it needs repeating in more people.

sections.title: Tests & biomarkers
sections.takeaway: There is still no validated lab test for ME/CFS, but several candidates look promising.

points.text: Blood tests based on DNA folding (96% accuracy in one test group) and on RNA fragments (about 77%) are the most advanced candidates; both still need wider testing.
Large blood-protein and ‘cell-particle’ studies find consistent differences, including work from the Scheibenbogen group.
Simple physical tests such as repeated hand-grip strength show real, measurable weakness and could track treatment effects, though they cannot diagnose on their own.
Patients seem to fall into subgroups — for example, a heavier-symptom group more often after an infection — but how to define them reliably is still open.

sections.title: Treatment: what has been tested
sections.takeaway: There is no approved drug for ME/CFS yet; several ideas show early promise, and several well-run trials were negative.

points.text: Early positive signals: the antibody-neutraliser BC007 in a placebo-controlled long-COVID trial, daratumumab in a small pilot, and hyperbaric oxygen in a Charité cohort (no placebo group). All need confirmation.
Clearly negative or disappointing: rituximab, Paxlovid, temelimab, immunoadsorption vs sham, and repurposed drugs that gave only a small, temporary benefit.

Exercise programmes can ease some symptoms but do not improve physical capacity, and patients rate graded exercise as least helpful. Better-organised care alone did not improve function in a Charité trial.
Trials often miss what patients actually rely on: only about 1 in 14 registered post-COVID trials test a patient-prioritised treatment, and few measure PEM as the main outcome.

sections.title: What to watch in Germany
sections.takeaway: Several German drug studies are open or planned — the Studies tab has eligibility details.

points.text: Open now: bupropion for post-COVID fatigue at up to 11 university hospitals, and two immunoadsorption studies for antibody-positive patients in Berlin and Potsdam.
Planned at Charité: B-cell therapy with inebilizumab for patients who responded to immunoadsorption and then relapsed, and low-dose aripiprazole.
Planned by Mitodicure (Klaus Wirth): the first human study of MDC002.
